Can I use TodoMode with Claude, Cursor or other AI assistants?

Yes. TodoMode runs a hosted MCP (Model Context Protocol) server at `https://app.todomode.com/mcp`. Connect Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or any other MCP client with a personal API token, and the assistant can see your projects and agenda, search, and — if you give it a read-and-write token — add, update and complete tasks. In Claude Code it is one command:

`claude mcp add --transport http todomode https://app.todomode.com/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer tm_…"`

When you create a token in Settings → API, TodoMode shows this command with your token filled in. A read-only token lets an assistant look but never change anything; deleted tasks go to the trash either way, and you can revoke a token at any time.

# The todomode command line

`todomode` puts TodoMode in your terminal: add a task without leaving the shell, list a project as an outline, tick things off by number, edit a note in your own editor, pipe a markdown list in. Everything has `--json` for scripts. It is one file with no dependencies beyond Python 3.8 or newer, which macOS (with the Command Line Tools) and almost every Linux already have.

...

Current version: 1.0.1.

## Everyday use #

```
todomode add "Fix login due:fri at:9am #work !high"       # to your Inbox
todomode add "Book flights due:next week" -p Travel       # to a project (a unique prefix is enough)
todomode add "Write tests" --under 3                      # as a subtask of #3 in the last listing

todomode ls                    # every project, open tasks, as outlines
todomode ls Work               # one project
todomode ls Work --all         # with completed tasks;  --done for only those
todomode ls --due overdue      # across projects; also --tag work, --priority high
```

octen.title: Show HN Guidelines
octen.snippet:
|   Show HN Show HN is for something you've made that other people can play with. HN users can try it out, give you feedback, and ask questions in the thread. On topic: things people can run on their computers or hold in their hands. For hardware, you can post a video or detailed article. For books, a sample chapter is ok. Off topic: blog posts, sign-up pages, newsletters, lists, and other reading material. Those can't be tried out, so can't be Show HNs. Make a regular submission instead. The project should be non-trivial. Don't post quickly-generated one-offs; anybody can do that now. Share something that is deeply personal and interesting to you. Explain how and why. The project must be something you've worked on personally and which you're around to discuss. See these tips about how to present your work. A Show HN needn't be complicated or look slick. The community is comfortable with work that's at an early stage. Please make it easy for users to try your thing out, ideally without barriers such as signups or emails. You'll get more feedback that way. If your work isn't ready for users to try out, please don't do a Show HN. Once it's ready, come back and do it then. Don't post landing pages or fundraisers. To post, submit a story whose title begins with "Show HN". Every Show HN appears on shownew. Once it clears a small points threshold, it will appear on the show page in the top bar. New features and upgrades ("Foo 1.3.1 is out") generally aren't substantive enough to be Show HNs. A major overhaul is probably ok. Please don't ask friends to upvote or comment. That's not ok on HN. In Comments Be respectful. Anyone sharing work is making a contribution, however modest. Ask questions out of curiosity. Don't cross-examine. Instead of "you're doing it wrong", suggest alternatives. When someone is learning, help them learn more. When something isn't good, you needn't pretend that it is, but don't be gratuitously negative.

我是一名来自东海岸的软件工程师（曾居住在波士顿、纽约、湾区、英国、法国），我打造了一个叫做 3 & Done 的任务系统。它是一个你可以信赖的地方，用来存储你所有需要做的事。它支持语音输入以快速录入，也支持文字输入（音频会本地保存，方便你回听来唤醒记忆），并且每天早上会给你发一封邮件，根据你对任务的描述——截止日期、紧急程度、搁置时间过长——告诉你当天最重要的三件事是什么，以及为什么。

OpenTodo is an open-source task manager designed for people who want a commercial-style productivity app without subscriptions or surrendering control of their data. Tasks can be captured in plain language, by voice, from a browser or phone share sheet, or by forwarding email; dates, priorities and projects can be assigned as part of the entry. The app supports daily and weekly planning with time estimates, focus timers, and shared projects with roles, task assignments and comments. Its web and mobile clients work offline, keeping a local copy of tasks and syncing after reconnecting. Users can also import tasks from services including Todoist, TickTick, Things and Microsoft To Do.
OpenTodo can run on a personal server, through managed hosting, in Docker, or as a single Go binary, with data stored locally in SQLite. The React-based app uses IndexedDB as its local source of truth; edits are synchronized through operations recorded by the server, with fields resolved using last-writer-wins. The project emphasizes data portability, scheduled backups, optional end-to-end encryption and privacy features such as no analytics or telemetry. It also offers an API, command-line client, browser extension, and integrations, plus optional AI assistance that is off by default. The software is licensed under AGPL-3.0 and aims to avoid lock-in: users can export their data and host the service themselves.

webiq.title: How to Launch on Hacker News: A Show HN Guide for 2026 | Shipyard
webiq.snippet:
- A Show HN is for something people can use right now, not a waitlist, a blog post, or a sign-up page.
- Post a plain "Show HN: name - description" title, explain what and why in the first comment, and never ask anyone to upvote.
- Post on a weekday US morning and stay in the thread for the next couple of hours; early replies and upvote velocity decide whether you hit the front page.
- Most Show HN posts get little traffic, and that's normal. Treat it as one channel for honest feedback, not a make-or-break event. ... Here is how to launch on Hacker News in one line: post a "Show HN" with a link people can actually use, add a first comment explaining what it is and why you built it, then stay in the thread and answer everyone.  ... A Show HN is a specific kind of submission, not a normal link with a label on it. It's for something people can try. "Something you've made that other people can play with," in HN's own words. Software they can run, a site they can use, a thing they can hold. ... It has to start with "Show HN:" followed by the name and a short description. Something like "Show HN: Fathom - offline maps for trail runners." Keep it plain. HN caps titles at 80 characters and asks you not to editorialize, so drop the adjectives and the exclamation marks.  ... A normal submission shares someone else's link. A Show HN shares your own working project and invites people to try it. It has to be something interactive people can run or use, so blog posts, newsletters, and sign-up pages don't qualify.

A weekday morning in the US, roughly Tuesday to Thursday between about 6 and 9am Pacific (9am to noon Eastern), when the technical crowd is active. There's no magic minute; showing up when the site is busy helps, because the front page runs on early upvote velocity.

Most posts get little traffic, but even a quiet Show HN usually brings sharp feedback from people who actually tried your thing, and a rare front-page run can send a real wave of users.
